topic: Geographic Perspectives: Global Change (Population Distribution, Global Climate, Global Resource Consumption)
subject: geography

items.title: Tropical cyclones need 26.5 °C sea surface temperatures
items.claim: What conditions are required for tropical cyclone formation?

options.text: Sea surface temperatures of at least around 26.5 °C, low vertical wind shear, sufficient distance from the equator (Coriolis force) and a pre-existing disturbance — typically 5-30° latitude

items.reveal:
Energy source: latent heat released as water vapour condenses. Tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator (insufficient Coriolis force to spin) and weaken rapidly over land or cool water.

Naming conventions: Atlantic/East Pacific = hurricanes; Northwest Pacific = typhoons; South Pacific/Indian Ocean = cyclones. Same phenomenon. The Saffir-Simpson scale (Category 1-5) classifies Atlantic and East Pacific storms by sustained wind speed.

Storm surge — wind-driven raising of sea level along the coast — is usually the deadliest hazard (Hurricane Katrina, 2005; Cyclone Bhola, 1970, killed at least 300,000 in East Pakistan).
items.why: Climate change is raising sea surface temperatures and expanding the zone where tropical cyclones can form and intensify. The deadliest hazard is also rising as warmer air holds more moisture.

items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: Fold mountains form at convergent plate boundaries

options.text: By the collision of the Indian and Eurasian continental plates, ongoing for around 50 million years and still uplifting at 5-10 mm/year
By erosion of a high plateau
By isostatic rebound from glacial retreat

items.reveal:
The Indian plate moved north at 15-20 cm/year through the Cenozoic — fast enough that the closure of the Tethys Ocean and collision with Eurasia produced the highest mountains on Earth.

Other active fold mountain systems: the Alps (Africa-Europe collision), the Andes (oceanic-continental subduction), the Caucasus, the Atlas. Older eroded systems: the Appalachians, the Caledonides (Scotland), the Urals.

India continues to push north at around 5 cm/year, still uplifting the Himalayas — and triggering many of the world's largest earthquakes along the Main Frontal Thrust.
items.why: Mountain building is active geology. The Himalayas are not static features but a still-unfolding consequence of plate motion — and the cause of regional seismic hazard.
